steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and state management capabilities.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main Auth component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Auth that returns null for now. This will be the main component for our authentication flow.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure to export it so it can be used elsewhere.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Auth component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named Auth is created and exported, returning null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the Auth component. This will serve as the foundation for our authentication flow.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a component named Auth that returns null and is exported.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating just the Auth component. Create a function named Auth that returns null for now.

steps.title: Initialize isLoggedIn state
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, use the useState hook to create a boolean state variable called isLoggedIn and initialize it to false.
steps.hint: Remember to use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is useState<boolean>(false).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Auth component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a state variable isLoggedIn with an initial value of false, ready to track authentication status.
successCriteria: The code includes a useState call inside the Auth component that declares isLoggedIn as a boolean state variable initialized to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isLoggedIn state variable. This will be used to track whether the user is authenticated.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be a small issue. Make sure you're using useState<boolean>(false) to properly type and initialize the state variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Remember to use the useState hook inside your Auth component to create a boolean state variable called isLoggedIn with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Initialize username state
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, add another useState hook to create a state variable called 'username' that will store a string. Initialize it with an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type <string> and pass an empty string as the initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a string state variable
const [username, setUsername] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The Auth component will have two state variables: isLoggedIn (boolean) and username (string).
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with <string> generic type, initialized to an empty string, and the variable should be named 'username'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a username state variable that will store the user's name as a string.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've used the correct generic type <string> and initialized it with an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The username state isn't properly initialized. Make sure you're using useState<string>('') to create a string state variable.

steps.title: Define handleLogin function
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, define an async function named handleLogin that simulates a login action. The function should set isLoggedIn to true and username to 'demoUser' after a 500ms delay.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the function, then inside use setTimeout with a callback that calls setIsLoggedIn and setUsername.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async handleLogin function that uses setTimeout to update both state variables after a delay.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the login handler that simulates an authentication delay.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is async, uses setTimeout, and updates both state variables correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleLogin function isn't defined correctly. Check if it's async, uses setTimeout, and updates both isLoggedIn and username.

steps.title: Define handleLogout function
steps.instruction: Inside your Auth component, define an async function named handleLogout that simulates logout by setting isLoggedIn to false and username to an empty string after a 500ms delay.
steps.hint: Create an async function that uses setTimeout to wait 500ms, then calls setIsLoggedIn(false) and setUsername('').
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async handleLogout function that uses setTimeout to simulate a delay before resetting the authentication state.
successCriteria: The function must be named handleLogout, be async, use setTimeout with 500ms delay, and call both setIsLoggedIn(false) and setUsername('').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the logout handler that simulates the logout process with a delay.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is async, uses setTimeout with 500ms, and calls both state setters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create an async function named handleLogout that waits 500ms before setting isLoggedIn to false and username to empty string.

steps.title: Return the main container div
steps.instruction: In your Auth component, return a div element with the className 'auth-container'.
steps.hint: Replace the existing return statement with a div that has the specified className.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Auth component now returns a div with className 'auth-container' as its main JSX structure.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element with className set to 'auth-container'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main container for your auth component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a div with exactly className='auth-container'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't return a div with className 'auth-container'. Check your return statement.

steps.title: Add conditional greeting display
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add a conditional that shows 'Welcome, {username}!' when isLoggedIn is true, otherwise show 'Please log in'.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator inside JSX to conditionally render different text based on the isLoggedIn state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component should conditionally display either 'Welcome, {username}!' when logged in or 'Please log in' when not logged in.
successCriteria: Add a ternary operator inside the container div that uses isLoggedIn to conditionally render the appropriate greeting text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering for the greeting based on authentication state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary operator with isLoggedIn to show different text in each branch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional greeting isn't implemented correctly. Check that you're using a ternary operator with isLoggedIn to show 'Welcome, {username}!' when true and 'Please log in' when false.

steps.title: Add login button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Login' inside the main container div. Set its onClick handler to call the handleLogin function, and add a disabled attribute that's set to true when isLoggedIn is true.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick={handleLogin} and disabled={isLoggedIn}. The button should be placed inside the existing <div> container.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a button wired to a handler with conditional disabling
<button onClick={handleClick} disabled={isDisabled}>
  Click me
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A login button appears in the UI that calls handleLogin when clicked and becomes disabled when the user is logged in.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the login button with proper click handling and conditional disabling.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your button has all three required elements: the text 'Login', onClick calling handleLogin, and disabled set to isLoggedIn.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't quite right. Check that you've added a <button> with the text 'Login', wired onClick to handleLogin, and set disabled based on isLoggedIn.

steps.title: Add logout button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Logout' inside your component's return statement. Wire its onClick event to call the handleLogout function and set its disabled attribute to disable the button when isLoggedIn is false.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick={handleLogout} and disabled={!isLoggedIn}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a logout button wired to a handler
<button onClick={handleLogout} disabled={!isLoggedIn}>
  Logout
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A logout button appears in the UI that calls handleLogout when clicked and is disabled when the user is not logged in.
successCriteria: The code must include a <button> element with text 'Logout', onClick={handleLogout}, and disabled={!isLoggedIn}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a logout button that's properly wired to the handler and conditionally disabled.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the button has all three required attributes: onClick, disabled, and the correct text content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The logout button is missing or incomplete. It needs to call handleLogout on click and be disabled when not logged in.

steps.title: Add loading state display
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element that displays 'Loading...' text. Place it inside the main container div, before the conditional greeting.

Use a

steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show a 'Loading...' paragraph at the top of the component, though it will always be visible for now.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the loading state display. In the next step, we'll make it conditionally appear only when login/logout is in progress.

steps.title: Initialize loading state and update handlers
steps.instruction: Initialize a loading state variable using useState with a boolean type and default value false. Then update both handleLogin and handleLogout functions to set loading to true at the beginning and to false after the setTimeout delay.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call for loading, then modify both handler functions to include loading state management.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a loading state that tracks async operations, and both login/logout handlers will properly manage this loading state.
successCriteria: 1. A loading state variable is initialized with useState<boolean>(false). 2. handleLogin sets loading to true at start and to false after setTimeout. 3. handleLogout sets loading to true at start and to false after setTimeout.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added loading state management to track async operations during authentication.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made progress, but check that: 1) loading state is initialized with boolean type, 2) both handlers set loading to true at the beginning, and 3) both handlers set loading to false after the setTimeout delay.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state management isn't complete. Make sure to initialize the loading state with useState, then update both handleLogin and handleLogout to manage the loading state throughout the async operations.
